header.title: What is autism?
header.subtitle: Autism is not an illness but a different course of development and a different way of perceiving. Learn how the spectrum works, explained by professionals in plain language.

traits.title: The diversity of how people function
traits.subtitle: No two autistic people are alike: abilities, challenges and strengths combine into a unique pattern.

items.title: Communication and social interaction
items.desc: Non-verbal signals, facial expressions, body language or metaphors can be hard to understand. Straightforward, honest and direct communication is typical.

items.title: Flexibility and predictability
items.desc: A familiar daily routine, a visual schedule and a structured environment give security. Unexpected changes can cause temporary tension.

items.title: Sensory sensitivity
items.desc: Sensory input (light, noise, touch, textures) is processed individually; both hypersensitivity and hyposensitivity occur on the spectrum.

myths.title: Facts and myths about autism
myths.subtitle: Breaking down prejudice starts with sharing correct and accurate knowledge.

items.myth: Autism is an illness that can be cured.
items.fact: Autism is not an illness but a neurodevelopmental difference. With the right early support and a supportive environment, the abilities of the people concerned can unfold.

items.myth: Autistic people do not want friends and have no feelings.
items.fact: They very much long for connection and have deep feelings; they simply need understanding in how social rules are expressed and interpreted.

items.myth: Every autistic person has extraordinary abilities (savant syndrome).
items.fact: Like everyone, people on the autism spectrum have individual profiles: each has their own strengths and areas where they need support.
A scientifically disproven myth. Autism goes back to a complex combination of genetic and biological factors and has nothing to do with parental care.

tips.title: Practical advice for affected parents
tips.subtitle: Based on PontMás's professional experience
items: Do not stay alone: join the parents' community of the PontMás Foundation, where you will find others who understand.
Identify your child's sensory needs (noise-cancelling ear defenders, soft lighting, comfortable clothes).
Use visual support: communication supported by pictures greatly reduces anxiety.
Focus on small successes and on your child's own strengths every day.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions (FAQ)
faq.subtitle: We have collected the most common questions, from diagnosis to development options.

items.question: What are the earliest signs of autism in early childhood?
items.answer: Rare eye contact, a delayed response to their name, missing shared attention (pointing), a stalled speech development and repetitive movements (e.g. flapping, lining things up) can be reasons to see a professional.

items.question: Where can I turn for a diagnostic assessment in Vas County?
items.answer: To the expert committee of the Vas County Pedagogical Service (Vas Vármegyei Pedagógiai Szakszolgálat), or, on the advice of the paediatrician or health visitor, to a child psychiatry clinic. Call us ({phone}) and we will gladly help you find your way through the process.

items.question: How can the family help shape the daily routine?
items.answer: Visual schedule cards (PECS, daily strips), advance notice (“we leave in 5 minutes”) and a low-stimulus quiet corner are proven to make everyday life run more smoothly.

items.question: What support does the PontMás Foundation give parents?
items.answer: We offer monthly parents' clubs, professional advice, help for institutions, summer camps and, in an exceptional crisis, direct financial support.

header.title: The story and mission of the PontMás Foundation
header.subtitle: Since 2015 we have built bridges between children on the autism spectrum, their families, professionals and society in Vas County.

story.title: Help born from personal commitment
story.p1: Our foundation was brought to life by life itself. Dedicated parents and special education teachers joined forces who had seen in everyday reality the obstacles a child on the autism spectrum and their family face in Vas County.
story.p2: We are not just an administrative organisation: we build a supportive community where parents can share their experiences and worries, and where children can develop in a safe, low-stimulus and loving setting.
story.nationalTitle: Part of the national professional network
story.aosz: Member organisation of the Hungarian Autistic Society (AOSZ)
story.board: The chair of the board of trustees is Edit Pohánka, who is also vice-president of the Hungarian Autistic Society (AOSZ). This position and recognised professional background ensure that our foundation supports the community in Vas County in line with national guidelines and the most up-to-date methods.

meta.ogDescription: Press articles, recognition and personal stories about the work of the PontMás Foundation.

articles.title: Szombathely dressed in blue – a walk and awareness on World Autism Day
articles.summary: With several hundred participants, affected families and supporters, the PontMás Foundation held the Blue Walk in Szombathely for World Autism Day. The blue lighting of the Town Hall and the main square stood for solidarity and acceptance.
articles.quote: “Our aim is for society to look at people on the autism spectrum not with fear or distance, but with openness and understanding.”

articles.title: “The parents' club gave us strength and something to hold on to during kindergarten inclusion”
articles.summary: A moving letter from a mother in Szombathely about how the PontMás Foundation's parents' club and the advice of trained special education teachers helped her little son start community life at the local kindergarten without difficulty.
articles.quote: “When we received the diagnosis, we felt isolated. The PontMás community not only answered every question professionally, we also found real security and friends.”

articles.title: The PontMás Foundation funded accredited training for special education teachers
articles.summary: Thanks to the municipal support of the City of Szombathely, 13 special education teachers and assistants in Szombathely took part in the 30-hour advanced professional training of the Autizmus Alapítvány (an autism foundation), funded 100% by our foundation.
articles.quote: “The best investment in our children's future is for the teachers who work with them every day to have the most up-to-date autism-specific methods.”

articles.title: Family Day and parents' club at the Vasi Skanzen open-air museum – community and recharging
articles.summary: At the traditional autumn family day the children enjoyed crafts, clay modelling, skittles and an obstacle course guided by special education teachers, while the parents shared their experiences in a support group led by a psychologist.
articles.quote: “The children could be themselves freely, without tension, and we parents could talk with relief about the challenges of everyday life.”

articles.badge: Thanks from an institution • Aranyhíd EGYMI
articles.title: New learning tools and a special library collection for autistic pupils
articles.summary: Special education teachers of local partner institutions thanked the PontMás Foundation for the donated visual schedule tools, sensory development toys and the growing specialist library.
articles.quote: “Without the foundation's support it would be much harder to give our pupils differentiated, personalised support.”
